title: The Debt Toll Booth: A Modular Solution to Addressing Sovereign Debt Crises
gist: David McNair argues that grand, consensus-based fixes to the developing-world sovereign debt crisis (like HIPC/MDRI) are politically impossible amid creditor fragmentation, fiscally strained G7 donors, a retrenching China and US-China friction in the G20. He proposes a modular 'toll booth' system with standardized lanes (liquidity, market access, solvency, concessional) convening only the minimum necessary stakeholders, and urges the UK's 2027 G20 presidency to champion it.

insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Breadth of distress signals elevated default and restructuring risk across frontier sovereign debt.

insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Borrowing costs above growth imply unsustainable debt dynamics absent relief or reform, pressuring frontier bond valuations.
insights.quote: The cost of borrowing for African countries increased by 91 percent from 2020 to 2024

insights.claim: Global official development assistance fell 23 percent in 2025, and the Iran war is projected to push an additional 45 million people into hunger through food price inflation, raising the urgency of the debt problem.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Falling aid plus food-price shocks reduce fiscal buffers in importing developing countries, increasing distress probability.
insights.quote: official development assistance (ODA)—which declined by 23 percent globally in 2025

insights.claim: Long-term external public and publicly guaranteed debt of low- and middle-income countries more than tripled from $1.11 trillion in 2000 to $3.56 trillion in 2024, fueled by cheap post-2008 borrowing and the commodity supercycle.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: The stock of EM sovereign debt exposed to refinancing risk is far larger than in the HIPC era.
insights.quote: Between 2000 and 2024, long-term external public and publicly guaranteed debt held by these countries more than tripled from $1.11 trillion to $3.56 trillion

insights.claim: Since 2020 low- and middle-income countries have absorbed successive shocks including COVID-19, the 2022 energy spike after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and the 2026 closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and McNair expects Africa's borrowing costs to keep rising.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Continued upward pressure on African sovereign spreads is the author's base case.
insights.quote: From 2020 to 2024, Africa’s borrowing costs increased by 91 percent, and are likely to continue their upward trajectory.

insights.claim: HIPC and MDRI debt relief delivered over $100 billion to thirty-seven countries, after which recipients spent about five times more on social services than on debt service, and sub-Saharan Africa grew 5.4 percent a year in 2000-2010 versus 1.4 percent for the G7.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Historical precedent suggests large-scale debt relief can unlock strong growth in recipient economies.
insights.quote: These initiatives delivered over $100 billion in debt relief for the thirty-seven participating countries.
insights.locator: A Recent History of Sovereign Debt

insights.claim: The G20 Common Framework has delivered relief equal to just 7 percent of at-risk lower-income countries' external debt, and only Chad, Ethiopia, Ghana and Zambia have used it because it is seen as slow, inefficient and unpredictable.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: The main official restructuring channel is ineffective, prolonging distressed-debt workouts and uncertainty for bondholders.
insights.quote: Only four countries—Chad, Ethiopia, Ghana, and Zambia—have sought restructuring under its auspices, due to a broadly shared perception of the framework as being slow, inefficient, and unpredictable.

insights.claim: The 2020 G20 Debt Service Suspension Initiative offered low-income countries a temporary reprieve on $12.9 billion of debt service but struggled to get private creditors on board.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Private creditor non-participation is a recurring weakness of official relief schemes.

insights.claim: The World Bank-IMF three-pillar approach backed by Brazil's 2024 G20 has shown no tangible success after nearly two years, partly because resulting financial flows went mainly to repaying creditors rather than supporting growth and reform.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: New money that merely refinances creditors does not restore fiscal space, so debt stress persists.
insights.quote: it has yet to demonstrate tangible success, in part because the resulting financial flows went mainly to repay creditors rather than to support growth and reform
insights.locator: In 2024, the G20 under the Brazilian

insights.claim: Using Claude Sonnet 4.6 to analyze G7 and G20 communiqué language from 2020 to 2026, McNair found donor commitment on sovereign debt peaked in 2022 and has since softened into a 'retrenchment' phase in 2025-2026.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Waning political will lowers odds of coordinated official relief for distressed sovereigns.
insights.quote: the author found that the strength of donor commitments to addressing sovereign debt peaked in 2022 and has since softened

insights.claim: The September 2026 G20 Finance Ministers meeting produced no communiqué after a US-China dispute, including over language on implementing the Common Framework and the three-pillar approach.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: US-China friction is now directly blocking multilateral debt coordination.
insights.quote: The September 2026 G20 Finance Ministers meeting resulted in a dispute between the United States and China

insights.claim: Three 2025 debt commissions (the Jubilee Report, the UN Secretary-General's Expert Group, and the Debt, Nature and Climate review) produced fifty overlapping recommendations that failed to gain political traction.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Technical policy proliferation without a political strategy yields little change, so investors should discount reform headlines.
insights.quote: These commissions, despite significant investment and deep expertise, have to date struggled to achieve political headway.

insights.claim: By 2024 bondholders had become the largest creditor group to low- and middle-income countries with $1.6 trillion, while China held $147.6 billion in bilateral lending plus $19.5 billion from its commercial banks.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Private bondholders now sit at the center of any restructuring, making their incentives decisive for recovery values.
insights.quote: by 2024, bondholders had become by far the largest creditor grouping, holding $1.6 trillion in debt to low- and middle-income countries

insights.claim: China is not a monolithic lender: its lending runs through Exim Bank, China Development Bank and several state-owned banks and insurers, and during COVID-19 Zambia owed money to eighteen different Chinese lenders.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Multiplicity of Chinese creditors with distinct incentives slows restructurings involving Chinese debt.
insights.quote: During the COVID-19 pandemic, Zambia’s government and state-owned firms collectively owed money to eighteen different Chinese lenders.
insights.locator: This fragmentation of the sovereign debt

insights.claim: Ethiopia's debt restructuring took more than three years, with proposals repeatedly rejected amid low trust in IMF forecasts and disputes over the comparability-of-treatment principle.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Comparability-of-treatment fights extend workout timelines, raising holding-period risk for distressed debt investors.
insights.quote: Such dynamics have taken center stage in Ethiopia’s debt restructuring negotiations, which took more than three years to complete.
insights.locator: This fragmentation of the debt landscape

insights.claim: Contrary to a common Western perception, China owns only 11.6 percent of Africa's overall debt and 4.8 percent of all low- and middle-income countries' external debt stock, even though it is Africa's largest bilateral creditor.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Undercuts the argument that Western relief would merely subsidize repayment to China, a key political blocker.
insights.quote: while China is Africa’s largest bilateral creditor, it owns just 11.6 percent of the continent’s overall debt

insights.claim: China's net flows to developing countries swung from $48 billion in 2010-2014 to negative $24 billion in 2020-2024 as debt service payments exceeded new lending.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: China has become a net extractor of capital from developing countries, worsening their external financing gaps.
insights.quote: China’s net flows to developing countries went from $48 billion between 2010 and 2014 to negative $24 billion between 2020 and 2024
insights.locator: Following the largesse of the Belt

insights.claim: China's property collapse wiped out local government land revenues and triggered a local government debt crisis, leading the China Development Bank to reorient from overseas infrastructure toward managing domestic restructuring and debt swaps.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Domestic stress reduces China's capacity and appetite to provide relief or new lending abroad.
insights.quote: China’s property collapse eliminated local government land revenues, producing a local government debt crisis.
insights.locator: Following the largesse of the Belt

insights.claim: Chinese overseas investment is increasingly driven by surplus industrial capacity in steel, solar, EVs and construction, pushing firms abroad on commercial rather than concessional terms; infrastructure lending fell from 75 percent to 25 percent of China's loan portfolio by 2023, replaced by liquidity support.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Signals Chinese overcapacity export push into emerging markets and a shift from project finance to rescue loans.
insights.quote: Chinese lending for infrastructure declined from 75 percent of its loan portfolio to 25 percent in 2023 and has been replaced by liquidity support facilities

insights.claim: By 2022, 60 percent of China's overseas lending was owed by borrowers in distress, incentivizing Chinese banks to extend bilateral rescue loans to preserve their portfolios.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Rescue lending can delay rather than resolve insolvencies, complicating coordinated restructurings.
insights.quote: by 2022, 60 percent of China’s overseas lending was owed by borrowers in distress

themes.theme: Donor fiscal strain and zero-sum politics

insights.claim: Average G7 debt-to-GDP rose from 74.6 percent in 2001 to 123.7 percent in 2026, with the UK's ratio tripling and the US's more than doubling, constraining donors' willingness to fund relief abroad.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Advanced-economy fiscal stress is now a binding constraint on global development finance.
insights.quote: Debt-to-GDP ratios for G7 members increased from an average of 74.6 percent in 2001 to 123.7 percent in 2026
insights.locator: Shifting Incentives and Challenges Facing Creditors

insights.claim: The US Congressional Budget Office projects a $3.4 trillion net increase in the US deficit over 2025-2034 and US sovereign debt above $52 trillion by 2035, with interest payments already exceeding Medicare and defense spending.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Rising US interest burden is a structural driver of Treasury supply and fiscal-policy risk.
insights.quote: Interest payments on this debt already exceed annual spending on Medicare, as well as national defense.

insights.claim: The G7 holds 41.2 percent of IMF votes, 39.7 percent at the World Bank's IBRD and 32.5 percent at IDA, so its domestic fiscal politics heavily shape multilateral debt outcomes.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Multilateral relief capacity tracks G7 political appetite, which is currently weak.
insights.quote: the G7’s vote share is 41.2 percent in the IMF, 39.7 percent in the World Bank’s International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, and 32.5 percent in the International Development Association

insights.claim: McNair argues that debt solutions tied to climate change are unlikely to win backing from the current US administration and that Chinese support for overhauling the debt architecture or boosting transparency may be hard to secure, ruling out a grand HIPC-style solution.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Investors should not expect a comprehensive global debt-relief deal in the near term.
insights.quote: Any debt solutions linked to climate change and sustainability, for instance, are unlikely to garner backing from the current U.S. administration.
insights.locator: A New Approach to Sovereign Debt Challenges

themes.theme: Borrower behavior and the sovereignty premium

insights.claim: Many developing countries now treat restructuring as a last resort and prioritize capital market access, sometimes choosing domestic austerity over default to protect market access.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Borrowers' default aversion supports eurobond payment continuity but at the cost of social spending and growth.
insights.quote: some countries have chosen to implement domestic austerity measures rather than default on their loans
insights.locator: In recent years, many low- and middle-income

insights.claim: African government domestic debt tripled from $150 billion to nearly $500 billion between 2010 and 2024 and has overtaken all other sources of public finance, meaning countries pay a 'sovereignty premium' of higher costs and shorter maturities for less exposure to external shocks.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Domestic debt is harder to restructure without hitting local banks, creating sovereign-bank doom-loop risk.
insights.quote: In short, countries have chosen to pay a sovereignty premium, assuming higher costs in return for reduced vulnerability to exogenous shocks
insights.locator: While this is a positive development

insights.claim: Eurobond borrowing is often poor long-term value versus multilateral development bank loans; ONE Data estimates $100 borrowed from IDA cost only $39 in present value in 2024, a $61 saving versus market terms.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Concessional MDB funding is far cheaper than market debt, so MDB capacity expansion matters for EM sovereign risk.
insights.quote: In 2024, every $100 borrowed from the World Bank’s International Development Association cost only $39 in present value, a savings of $61 compared with market-equivalent borrowing.

insights.claim: Only one in four low-income countries discloses loan-level information on newly contracted debt, and hidden-debt episodes like Mozambique's tuna bonds and Senegal's 2025 audit revisions show opacity can abruptly cut off market access.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Hidden-debt revelations are a key tail risk for frontier sovereign spreads.
insights.quote: An audit published in February 2025 revealed substantial revisions to fiscal deficits and public debt from 2019 to 2023, triggering a sharp increase in sovereign spreads

insights.claim: Debt sustainability depends on what debt finances: a country borrowing at 9 percent for investment with higher fiscal returns differs fundamentally from one borrowing at the same rate to refinance legacy obligations or fund recurrent spending.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Credit analysis should weigh public investment efficiency, not just headline debt ratios.
insights.quote: The development return on borrowed capital varies enormously by country and with the quality of the domestic institutions managing expenditure.

insights.claim: McNair proposes a modular 'toll booth' system where distressed countries enter standardized lanes with predictable, time-bound treatments and transparent quantitative triggers, convening only the minimum necessary stakeholders rather than seeking G20 consensus.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Standardized treatments would make restructuring outcomes more predictable, aiding pricing of distressed sovereign debt.
insights.quote: This kind of country segmentation could create a standardized “toll booth” approach, whereby countries enter different lanes and can expect standardized treatment based on the situation they face.
insights.locator: A Modular Approach to Debt Challenges

insights.claim: The Finance for Development Lab classifies low- and lower-middle-income countries as seven insolvent, twenty-three solvent but liquidity-constrained, and twenty-eight low-risk.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: Most stressed sovereigns face liquidity rather than solvency problems, favoring refinancing over haircuts.
insights.quote: seven countries are deemed to be “insolvent”; twenty-three are considered “solvent but face liquidity constraints”; and another twenty-eight are “low-risk.”
insights.locator: As analysis from the Finance for Development Lab

insights.claim: The proposed lanes are a fast liquidity lane (debt service suspensions, MDB debt swaps), a medium market-access lane, a slow solvency lane for restructuring including a Spain-backed Jubilee buy-back fund, and a concessional lane resembling a modern HIPC/MDRI.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: A buy-back fund refinancing high-cost debt via MDBs could support secondary prices of distressed bonds.
insights.quote: This could include the rapid implementation of a Jubilee buy-back fund, as championed by the government of Spain, to purchase high-cost debt and refinance it at lower rates

insights.claim: McNair cites the G20's Capital Adequacy Framework work as proof that small expert-led coalitions can deliver, noting it unlocked $400 billion in MDB lending headroom.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: MDB balance-sheet optimization is a proven lever to expand development lending without new capital.
insights.quote: The subsequent action from the governors and management of MDBs unlocked $400 billion in lending headroom from the MDB system.

insights.claim: McNair predicts the UK's 2027 G20 presidency, followed by its 2028 G7 hosting, is the main near-term opening for structural debt reform and urges the UK to engage China and private creditors in codesigning a segmented approach.
insights.speaker: David McNair
insights.so_what: The 2027 UK G20 is a catalyst date for potential sovereign debt architecture changes.
insights.quote: Early indications signal an appetite from the UK government to use its presidency to address the issue in a structural way.
